title: How To Stop Misbehavior Before It Starts
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes how experienced teachers can often sense an approaching bad day before misbehavior actually breaks out, and offers a step-by-step protocol for acting on that intuition rather than dismissing it as bad luck. The routine involves stopping students in their tracks, calling for one minute of silence, using the phrase 'in a moment' to segue into directions, and then having students restart a routine — such as the arrival procedure — from the beginning without lengthy explanation. He stresses that this reset only works if routines were thoroughly modeled and practiced beforehand, and that teachers should avoid lecturing, since action communicates expectations far more powerfully than words. The piece closes by rejecting common excuses (weather, holidays, day of the week) for early-warning misbehavior.
points: Teachers often sense early warning signs of a difficult day and should act on that intuition rather than shrugging it off as inevitable.
The reset protocol involves stopping students, calling for one minute of silence, then using the phrase 'in a moment' before restarting a routine from the beginning.
This strategy only works if the underlying routine was already modeled and practiced thoroughly with students beforehand.
Teachers should avoid explaining or lecturing during the reset — action, not words, communicates expectations most powerfully.
Common excuses for whole-class restlessness (weather, holidays, day of the week) are rejected; students can behave regardless of external circumstances.
quotes: Whether or not you’re able pinpoint the source of your uneasiness doesn’t matter. What matters is how you respond.
But to be an effective teacher, to create the peaceful, well-behaved class you really want, you can ill afford to lose a single day settling for less than the best from your students.
The phrase “in a moment,” best used just prior to giving directions, is an effective way to keep your students from moving on mentally or physically before you’ve finished talking.

What you do is infinitely more important than what you say. Thus, performing routines over again is a powerful classroom management strategy that communicates to students all they need to know to get themselves back on track.
Five minutes of action will reinforce your expectations more effectively and more profoundly than anything you can say.
Because students can behave how you want, they can be calm and attentive—regardless of what day of the week it is or what’s happening outside the four walls of your classroom.
